messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 46
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Forensic Analyst
- Trauma Type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
- Pcl5: 78

She is 46, married, and works as a forensic analyst, a job that once fit her mind neatly. She has always been someone who trusts evidence, sequence, and detail. Before her life split into a before and after, she describes herself as steady, private, and capable of holding difficult material at work without bringing it home. She spends her days reconstructing other people’s worst moments from fragments—fibers, photographs, timelines, blood spatter, inconsistencies that tell the truth when witnesses cannot. For years, she believes that careful observation can make terrible things comprehensible.

The event that undoes this belief is the sudden death of her younger brother. He dies unexpectedly in a boating accident during a family holiday. One moment he is laughing on the dock, teasing her about checking the weather report twice, and the next there is shouting, then the frantic confusion of people running, then the awful stretch of time in which nobody can say exactly where he is. She remembers details with painful sharpness: the chemical smell of fuel, the slap of water against wood, her sister-in-law screaming his name until her voice breaks. She also remembers moments that feel unreal, as if her mind records them but never fully accepts them. By the time his body is found, she is already moving into a kind of cold efficiency, calling relatives, answering questions, noticing who needs to be driven home. She hates herself for how quickly that professional part of her takes over.

In the weeks after the funeral, she does not cry as much as people expect. Instead she becomes consumed by the mechanics of his death. She asks for the incident report, reads it repeatedly, and searches for discrepancies. At night she replays the scene in loops, constructing alternate sequences in which he is saved. If someone had checked the engine. If she had insisted they come in earlier. If she had stood closer to the edge. Sleep becomes shallow and broken. She wakes with her heart racing, convinced for a few seconds that she can still do something. Her husband reaches for her in the dark and she startles so violently that he pulls back. She tells him she is fine, but begins sleeping turned away from him, tense and listening.

As months pass, reminders are everywhere and nowhere predictable. The smell of salt water in a grocery store parking lot, a news story about a marine rescue, a child shouting across a beach—each can pull her abruptly back into that day. When it happens she is no longer fully in the present. Her chest tightens, her skin goes cold, and for a moment she hears her brother’s name being called over open water. She avoids the coast entirely, though she grew up near it and once found it calming. Family gatherings become difficult because his absence feels louder than conversation. She stops answering her sister-in-law’s messages for weeks at a time, then feels ashamed and sends formal, overcareful replies that sound nothing like herself.

Her work changes too. In the lab she remains technically excellent, but the distance she once kept from violent death is gone. Cases involving drowning or accidental fatalities leave her shaky and nauseated. She studies photographs too long, then cannot bear to look at them. Colleagues notice she is slower with reports and more irritable when interrupted. She begins double- and triple-checking every chain-of-custody form, seized by the fear that one small oversight could ruin everything. She stays late to review files she has already reviewed, unable to trust her own conclusions. At home, she cannot explain why sorting laundry or hearing the dishwasher hum suddenly feels overwhelming after spending all day examining evidence.

She has become increasingly watchful in ordinary life. When her husband drives, she monitors speed, weather, road conditions, hazards that are still far ahead. If he is ten minutes late coming home, she imagines police at the door. She keeps her phone volume on high through the night and panics if she misses a call. There are times she knows her mind is making impossible leaps, but knowledge does not stop the surge of dread. She says she is exhausted by “living as if disaster is always just ahead of me.”

What troubles her most is not only grief, but the sense that she no longer recognizes herself. She used to believe she could tolerate uncertainty; now uncertainty feels cruel and unbearable. She used to be warm with her husband, funny with friends, the one who remembered birthdays and checked in on everyone. Now she withdraws, cancels plans, and sits through dinners half absent, tracking exits and trying not to react to ordinary noises. She often feels detached, as if there is glass between her and other people’s lives. On better days she can talk about her brother and remember his humor. On worse days she avoids even saying his name, because once the images start, they come with full force and do not loosen their grip for hours.

By the time she speaks openly about it, she is carrying a constant mixture of guilt, fear, anger, and numbness. She says she knows her brother is dead, but some part of her remains fixed on the dock, still listening for the splash, still waiting for the moment when the day can be rewritten.
